## Destructive action state contract

### Decision sequence

1. **Availability first.** Determine whether the selected record may be deleted and expose the reason and corrective action when it may not.
2. **Input feedback second.** Pointer hover, keyboard focus, and press are visual feedback only; they never change deletion eligibility or operation state.
3. **Commit atomically.** On the first valid activation, set `isSubmitting` before starting the request. This moves the control to loading and rejects every later pointer, keyboard, or programmatic invocation until the request settles.
4. **Resolve locally.** Success removes or marks only the affected record; failure keeps its context and exposes an adjacent retry path. Neither outcome creates a page-level empty state.

### State model

**Semantic operation state** is `ready`, `unavailable`, `submitting`, `succeeded`, or `failed`. It is driven only by permission/selection rules and request lifecycle events. **Visual interaction state** is `default`, `hover`, `focus-visible`, or `pressed`; it is driven by pointer position, keyboard/programmatic focus, and pointer/keyboard press. A visual state may coexist with `ready`, but never substitutes for an operation state.

Use the existing semantic token families for destructive foreground/surface/border, focus indicator, disabled content, success feedback, error feedback, and motion. Do not substitute raw colors or opacity alone; every treatment also has a text, icon, or structural cue.

| state and trigger | status | reason | remediation | evidence | provenance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ready` semantic state; selection is deletable and no request is active | pass | The action is available without implying it is harmless. | Render the native destructive `<button>` with its existing destructive token treatment and a clear accessible name such as `Delete selected record`. | `disabled` is absent; the activation handler accepts input only while `isSubmitting === false`. | Native button semantics; existing destructive semantic tokens. |
| `hover` visual state; fine pointer enters a ready button | pass | Hover confirms pointer affordance but is not required to discover or use the control. | Apply the existing destructive-hover token and preserve the label/icon; do not reveal essential instructions only on hover. | `:hover` is scoped to hover-capable pointers and does not change `aria-*` attributes or operation state. | Component-state hover invariant; semantic hover token. |
| `focus-visible` visual state; Tab navigation or programmatic keyboard-style focus reaches a ready button | pass | Keyboard users need an unambiguous current target that does not depend on pointer hover. | Apply a visible focus ring with the existing focus token and offset; never remove the outline without this replacement. | `:focus-visible` is present and remains visible against the destructive surface at required UI contrast. | WCAG focus-visible requirement; existing focus semantic token. |
| `pressed` visual state; pointer down, Space, or Enter activation is in progress | pass | Immediate acknowledgement prevents an otherwise inert-feeling destructive action. | Use the existing fast-motion token for a brief transform or surface change; remove it when the key/pointer releases and respect reduced motion. | `:active` or equivalent press state is visual only and lasts roughly the existing fast-duration range. | Component-state active-feedback invariant; existing motion tokens. |
| keyboard activation; focused ready button receives Enter or Space | pass | Keyboard invocation must have the same result and guard as pointer activation. | Keep the native button; use no click-only custom handler. Enter/Space invoke the same guarded command, and Tab order remains unchanged. | Browser-native button keyboard behavior reaches the same `beginDelete` path as a click. | Native HTML button interaction model. |
| `unavailable` semantic state; permission, protected status, or missing selection prevents deletion | pass | A disabled control without a reason is a dead end, especially in a dense toolbar. | Set native `disabled`; show persistent nearby text explaining why and, when applicable, the control or link that restores eligibility. Do not use `aria-disabled` in place of native `disabled` for this button. | The control has `disabled`; its explanation remains available without hover and names the prerequisite or protection. | Native disabled semantics; existing disabled semantic tokens. |
| `submitting` semantic state; the first guarded activation has set `isSubmitting = true` | pass | Async work must be perceptible and must not permit duplicate destructive requests. | Set `disabled`, change the accessible button label to `Deleting…`, show a spinner plus text, and set `aria-busy="true"` on the affected row or nearest results region. Clear busy only when the request settles. | State transition is atomic before the request; subsequent Enter, Space, click, and programmatic calls return early while `isSubmitting` is true. | Async-action invariant; native disabled semantics; ARIA busy state; existing loading tokens. |
| no-double-submit guard; any activation while `submitting` | pass | Disabled styling alone is not a concurrency control. | Make the request owner reject re-entry with `if (isSubmitting) return`; keep the button disabled until its own request resolves, including slow-network cases. | One transition from `ready` to `submitting` owns one request; later events create zero additional requests. | Async state-machine guard. |
| `succeeded` semantic state; deletion request resolves successfully | pass | Completion must be announced and leave focus on a useful surviving target. | Update only the affected record, announce `Record deleted` through a nearby `role="status"` region, then move focus to the next logical row action or the toolbar if no sibling remains. If undo is the recovery mechanism, render an explicit, keyboard-focusable `Undo` control in that same persistent status area until its expiry; never make it hover-only or toast-only. | Busy is cleared; the deleted row is gone or marked deleted; the success status and any Undo control are visible in the local interface. | Live-region success pattern; focus-order invariant; existing success semantic tokens. |
| `failed` semantic state; deletion request rejects or returns an error | pass | The user needs the record context, an explanation, and a recoverable next action rather than a vanished or silently reset control. | Clear `aria-busy`, restore an enabled destructive button labelled `Retry deletion`, retain the selected record, and render an adjacent error message with `role="alert"` that includes the failure reason where safe. Keep the Retry control visible and keyboard reachable; do not replace the results area with an empty-state treatment. | The error message, Retry control, and original record context coexist; keyboard focus remains on the trigger or is deliberately moved to the alert only when that is necessary to make the new error actionable. | Error-recovery pattern; live alert semantics; existing error semantic tokens. |

### Invariants

- `aria-busy` belongs to the affected row or compact results region during submission; the button uses native `disabled` to communicate and enforce unavailability.
- The request guard is shared by mouse, touch, keyboard, and programmatic entry points, so visual pressed feedback cannot create a second request.
- Focus never falls to `body`: after success it lands on a logical surviving control; after failure the visible Retry path remains in the local record context.
- Every state treatment uses the existing semantic tokens, meets state contrast requirements, and pairs color with a label, icon, outline, or structural change.

## Async destructive action contract

Use one real `<button type="button">` for the destructive action. Its visual state is a presentation of the semantic state; it must never be the source of truth. Use the existing semantic destructive, destructive-hover, focus, disabled, success, error, surface, and fast-motion tokens—no literal colors or replacement palette.

| Semantic state | Trigger and ownership | Visual state | Behavior and semantics | Exit / recovery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ready | The item is eligible and no request is in flight. Owned by the action controller. | Destructive button at rest. Hover uses the existing destructive-hover token; active/pressed uses the fast motion token and a small transform. | Pointer click and `Enter`/`Space` invoke the same guarded submit function. `:focus-visible` draws the existing focus token with a visible offset; hover is never the only affordance. | Submit begins only after the guard accepts it. |
| Pending confirmation | A destructive action requires explicit confirmation. Owned by the confirmation dialog. | Trigger remains identifiable behind the dialog; confirm is visually destructive, cancel is always visible. | Move focus into the dialog, keep it contained while open, and return focus to the trigger on cancel. `Escape` cancels when safe; `Enter` confirms only when the confirm button has focus. | Cancel returns to Ready. Confirm enters Submitting. |
| Submitting | The guarded submit function has accepted one request. Owned by the request lifecycle. | Button shows a spinner and a specific label such as “Deleting…”, using the existing disabled/loading treatment. | Set `aria-busy="true"` on the smallest affected action region and native `disabled` on the submit control. For an `aria-disabled` custom control, block activation in code as well. The guard rejects all pointer, keyboard, and repeated programmatic submissions while this request key is pending. | Resolve to Succeeded or Failed; do not time out into an unexplained disabled state. |
| Succeeded | The server confirms the action. Owned by the response handler. | Replace loading with an inline success message near the affected row or action region; announce it through a polite status region. | Remove busy/disabled semantics. If the action is reversible, keep an Undo action visible for its real availability window; otherwise state the completed result plainly. | End at the post-action local UI state; do not invent a page-level empty state. |
| Failed | The request rejects or returns an error. Owned by the response handler. | Show an inline error treatment adjacent to the action, with an error icon plus text—not color alone. Keep the destructive trigger available once the request ends. | Clear `aria-busy` and native `disabled`. Announce the error in an assertive error region. Preserve the failed item and any entered context. | Leave a visible Retry action and, when applicable, a visible alternate recovery path such as “Check permissions” or “Contact support”; never hide the only recovery path in a toast, overflow menu, or vanished dialog. |

### Interaction rules

- **Keyboard parity:** tab reaches the trigger; `Enter` and `Space` produce the same confirmation/request path as a pointer click. Focus is always visible through `:focus-visible`; no `outline: none` without the tokenized replacement.
- **Pressed feedback:** `:active` is immediate and transform-based, uses the existing fast-duration token, and is removed under reduced-motion preferences. It indicates registration only; it does not claim completion.
- **Disabled versus unavailable:** use native `disabled` only during submission or when the action truly cannot run. If prerequisites are missing, keep a route to the explanation or recovery adjacent to the action rather than offering a silent grey control.
- **No double submit:** the controller creates one request key before dispatch; the key is cleared only in a single `finally` path. The visual loading state, native disabled state, and request guard must change together.

### Acceptance ledger

| Status | Reason | Remediation | Evidence | Provenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pass | Visual and semantic state are distinct: Ready, Pending confirmation, Submitting, Succeeded, and Failed are lifecycle facts; hover, focus-visible, active, disabled, and loading are their presentation. | Implement one controller-owned state machine and bind visual attributes to it. | The state table names a trigger, owner, visual treatment, semantics, and exit for every state. | Component-state contract for this destructive action. |
| Pass | Keyboard users need the same path and a visible location indicator, while an async request needs both machine-readable busy state and interaction blocking. | Use native button semantics, `:focus-visible`, `aria-busy`, native `disabled`, and the shared request key. | Interaction rules explicitly cover Tab, Enter, Space, focus-visible, aria-busy, disabled, and the no-double-submit guard. | Accessibility and async lifecycle requirements for this control. |
| Pass | Success must confirm a completed action; failure must preserve the item and its recovery route without changing the whole page into an empty state. | Place success/error feedback beside the action region and retain Retry or the applicable alternate recovery action. | Succeeded and Failed rows define local status announcements, restoration of interactivity, and visible recovery. | Response-handling contract for this destructive action. |
| Pass | A state contract must be auditable rather than a list of checkmarks. | Keep the acceptance ledger with a result, rationale, prescribed fix, observable proof, and source context. | Each ledger row contains Status, Reason, Remediation, Evidence, and Provenance. | Review record embedded in this contract. |
